How the numbers work

Each team gets an attack rating from goals scored and a defence rating from goals conceded, worked out match by match: three goals against the league leaders count for more than three against the bottom side, and recent matches count a little more than ones from August. Where a match has expected goals (xG), the ratings use half goals and half xG, which takes some of the luck out; where it doesn't, shots on target stand in for xG. Every team starts from ratings worked out the same way from all of last season's matches, and this season's games take over as they build up: after about 20 games, this season counts for half. Promoted teams start from how they did in the division below, scaled down a step, and relegated teams from the division above, scaled up. Points per game and last weekend's result tilt the numbers slightly.

Home attack against away defence, and the reverse, plus home advantage, set each side's expected goals. Home advantage starts at roughly 0.3 goals and is adjusted for each league as its results are scored. A Poisson model turns those into every likely scoreline, which sum to the home win, draw and away win chances, allowing for the fact that the ratings are estimates. The stats model is then blended with a second opinion that knows things results can't, like squad quality and injuries, with the second opinion counting for 95% because replaying last season and this one (about 9,700 matches) showed the bookmakers are the harder benchmark to beat: bookmaker odds converted to probabilities (with the bookmaker's margin removed) in every league, plus the data feed's probabilities in the five top leagues. When a match has a bookmakers' over/under 2.5 goals line, the expected goals are scaled towards it, which sharpens the likeliest scores, both-teams-to-score and over 2.5 figures. A pick is marked strong at 60% or more.

The Premier League, La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 come from a live sports data feed. The Championship, League One, League Two, National League, Segunda División, Serie B, 2. Bundesliga and Ligue 2, plus the four Scottish divisions, the Eredivisie, Belgian Pro League, Primeira Liga, Süper Lig and Greek Super League, come from published league tables, results and fixture lists. Each match card shows the date its table is from, and a league whose table is more than a week old is marked "old table".

Each match card shows the stats model and the second opinion side by side, so you can see where they disagree. Football is noisy: a 60% favourite still fails to win four times in ten. For fun, not for staking money.

How the darts picks work

Every PDC match this year and last (TV events, the European Tour, the World Series, the Premier League and every round of every Players Championship) feeds a rating for each player, based on the legs they win and lose against whoever they play, with recent matches counting more. That's blended with each player's recent three-dart average. A player's chance of winning a match then follows from the format: first to six legs swings more than first to sixteen.

Players Championship results come from Mastercaller, every round. Some players raise their game on TV stages and others shrink, so each player also has a stage adjustment, learned from the gap between their stage and floor results and kept small unless the evidence is strong. "Leg win %" in the ratings table is a player's chance of winning a leg against an average tour player, on stage and on the floor. There are no free bookmaker prices for darts, so these picks come from the ratings alone, and darts isn't in Auto bet. Session times (UK) come from Mastercaller's order of play, usually a few days before each event; until then matches show the day of their round. "Who wins" plays out the rest of a knockout draw 20,000 times using these ratings.

Bet only what you can afford to lose. Free help: BeGambleAware.org.

How the snooker picks work

Every ranking and invitation event this season and last that Wikipedia lists feeds a rating for each player, based on the frames they win and lose against whoever they play, with recent matches counting more. A player's chance of winning a match then follows from its length: a best-of-7 swings far more than a best-of-19 or the World Championship's best-of-35 final. "Who wins" plays out the rest of a knockout draw 20,000 times.

"Frame win %" in the ratings table is a player's chance of winning a frame against an average tour player. There are no free bookmaker prices for snooker, so these picks come from the ratings alone, and snooker isn't in Auto bet. Times aren't listed; matches show the day of their round. Tested on 950 matches this year, each predicted before it was played: the favourite won 67% of the time, and strong picks (70% or more) 76%.

Bet only what you can afford to lose. Free help: BeGambleAware.org.

How the auto bets work

Each strong pick gets the same stake at Bet365's pre-match odds, taken from football-data.co.uk. A win pays the stake times the odds minus the stake; a loss loses the stake. Picks with no Bet365 price in the data, such as most cup ties, are left out. Live picks are the ones Pitch Oracle saved before kick-off; the season replay adds this season's earlier matches, picked by the model using only what was known before each match.

A 6-fold acca takes the six strongest picks of one day (60% or more, or 65% or more if you choose) that have Bet365 odds, multiplies their odds together, and only pays if all six win. Days with fewer than six priced strong picks get no acca. Accas pay more when they land but lose far more often, because one wrong leg sinks the lot.

Past results don't guarantee future ones, and bookmakers' margins make long-run profit hard. Free help: BeGambleAware.org.

About the bet log

Profit counts settled bets only. "Beat the closing odds" compares the odds you took with the price just before kick-off; doing that more often than not is the best sign of good betting, even through a losing run. Paper bets let you test an idea without staking anything.

Set a limit you're happy to lose. Free help and tools: BeGambleAware.org and GamCare.

Every pick is saved before the first serve and scored once the match finishes. The first scores appear after today's matches.

How the numbers work

Every pick starts from each player's Elo rating from Tennis Abstract, built from every tour and Challenger result: beating a top player lifts it more than beating someone ranked 200th. There's a separate rating for hard courts, clay and grass, each mixed with the overall one, and between Tennis Abstract's weekly updates each result nudges both players' ratings a little. A 100-point gap is about 64%, 200 about 76%. Men's Grand Slam matches are best of five, which helps the better player, so those chances are stretched.

Where there's a betting market it's blended in and counts for most of the pick. Prices come from two prediction markets, Kalshi and Polymarket, averaged when both price a match; Polymarket also covers most Challenger and WTA 125 matches. Prices are re-read four times a day, so most picks are set within a few hours of the start, when prices are sharpest. Replaying every ATP and WTA tour match of 2024, 2025 and 2026 (about 15,000 matches) showed why: the market's favourite won 68–69% of the time, against 65–66% for ratings alone, because the market already knows about injuries, illness and withdrawals. The replay also set three smaller adjustments: indoor hard courts weigh each player's indoor record; playing more matches in the last week is a small plus (it usually means good form, not tiredness); and coming back from a break of six weeks or more is a small minus. Without a market, a games-won rating also counts a little for the men: winning 6–1 6–2 says more than 7–6 7–6.

The replay's 2026 test showed the numbers are honest: matches picked at 70–80% were won 75–77% of the time. A pick is marked strong at 75% or more. The track record also shows how the market alone and the ratings alone would have done on the same picks. Only singles are shown, and only when both players have a rating (roughly the top 330 men and women). For fun, not for staking money.
